item.title: In a world of panic, calm and certainty win
item.description: You can dread the future or help build it. The people who come through this already chose.While panic around what AI means for our industry is the reflex right now, calm is a decision. The calm that comes from knowing what you actually know is the rarest and most valuable thing you can bring to a moment like this.I recently turned 50 and reckoning with that did what it does to so many people. It made me think. Not in a hauntingly dramatic, staring-out-the-window way, but in an introspective way where you start taking stock of what you’ve actually learned, what still rattles you, and what has stopped rattling you entirely.That thinking rooted itself from a conversation I had with Skift founder Rafat Ali. When he found out my birthday was coming, he got genuinely excited for me, which is not how most people react to 50. He told me the day after my birthday would be the best day of my life, because that’s when you get to put the whole thing behind you. He said that you just stop carrying the pressure you put on yourself and the pressure you imagine everyone else is putting on you.That conversation quickly moved on from my age and on to work, to his industry and to what AI is doing to all of it. Without noticing, Rafat said the same thing again in a completely different context.“There’s so much uncertainty,” he told me, “that the people who stay calm and certain are the ones everyone listens to. In a moment where nobody knows what’s happening, calm is the whole advantage.”I haven’t stopped thinking about that since.Those two pieces of advice are actually one piece of advice. The relief Rafat promised me about 50, the freedom of putting down the need to prove yourself, is the exact thing that makes a person valuable in a moment like this one.The whole industry is panicking about AI. The people who come out of it fine will be the ones who already learned how to put the panic down.The fear is real, widespread, and not at all stupid. That’s exactly why it’s worth handling well.The fear is realThe numbers are striking.Pew Research found that 71 percent of Americans now think AI will mean fewer jobs over the next twenty years, up from 64 percent two years earlier, and among adults under 30 it’s 73 percent. Pew is careful to note that number reflects what people expect, not jobs that have actually been lost.ADP’s global study of more than thirty-nine thousand people, led by their chief economist Nela Richardson, found that anxiety, not confidence, is now the defining feeling workers have about their work.A survey from the Sylvia Brafman Mental Health Center found nearly half of workers say AI worry has hurt their mental health, climbing to two in three among the youngest polled.It has gotten real enough that it’s showing up in doctors’ offices. Dr. Simbiat Adighije described a patient who couldn’t stop checking the news, couldn’t stop imagining which parts of her job and her identity might be automated next, and made a point worth holding ontoThe anxiety is real whether or not the prediction driving it ever comes true, the same way climate anxiety is legitimate no matter what you think of any particular model.This isn’t in your head. The ground is actually moving, and anyone who says otherwise is lying to your face.Look closely at that Pew number, though, because it’s quite telling. The dread is at an all-time high, and it’s a forecast, a thing people expect, running well ahead of what has actually happened to them. That gap, between how frightened people are and what has actually changed in their own working lives, is where panic lives.Fear and panic are not the same thing. Fear is a reasonable response to a real risk. Panic is what happens when the fear starts making your decisions for you.The clinical psychologist Zachary Sikora says that fear is literally our survival response, useful, hardwired, and designed to keep us alive. When it spikes, however, it impairs the part of the brain that handles reasoning and judgment, the exact faculties you need most when things are uncertain.The more afraid you get, the worse you think.Every disruption runs the same arc. The panic always comes, and whether it takes you is up to you.We have seen this exact panic beforeEvery big technological shift runs the same arc.Dora Czerna traced it across decades of disruptions and named the stages. First comes democratization, when a tool suddenly lets a lot more people do something that used to take an expert. Then comes panic, when the experts realize it. Then a stretch of genuine quality collapse, when all those new people flood the zone with mediocre work. Eventually, new norms settle in, and the field is bigger and different and mostly fine.When desktop publishing arrived, it gave us a decade of ransom-note flyers with twelve fonts on them, and then it gave us a generation of designers who could do more than any typesetter ever could.The panic comes for everyone. Whether you give in to it is up to you.This isn’t simply a modern problem. Calestous Juma, who spent years studying how societies react to new technology, found the same pattern running back six hundred years. Coffee, refrigeration, mechanized farming, electricity, every one of them met a wave of fear and resistance before it became ordinary.The fear, he found, was rarely really about the technology, but rather about people sensing they might lose a piece of their identity or their livelihood, feeling it first and reaching for the evidence afterward.Economist Derek Thompson has pointed out that the single strongest argument for AI not causing some overnight jobs apocalypse is one word, history. New technology has been reshaping work for centuries, and the story is always the same. The technology shows up, the work changes, and it almost always goes slower and messier than anyone predicted in the panic.I’ve certainly experienced my own smaller versions of this. The web was going to make everyone a designer, and then it didn’t. The bootcamps were going to flood the field and end the profession, and then they didn’t.Every time this happens, the panic feels like the end of something, and every time it turns out to be the loud, ugly middle of something, the part right before the new normal shows up and everyone forgets they were ever that scared.Panic in a downturn is the go-to emotion, even at the top. Nancy Koehn, who studies how leaders handle crises, points to research showing that more than half of leaders become more closed-minded and controlling when a crisis hits, and more than four in ten get angrier and more reactive. The steadiness we remember in the leaders who got it right, the Lincolns and the Shackletons, was always the rare response, which is exactly why it resonates so well.None of this means the fear is wrong. It means the fear is a stage, and stages pass, especially for the people who don’t let it take over.The calm that wins is the kind you earn, from knowing what you’re good at and no longer needing to prove it.The calm that wins is the kind you earnThere’s a version of calm that’s just denial, the person insisting nothing is changing while the ground shifts under them. Plugging your ears with your fingers, screaming “la la la la la,” hoping the phase just passes you by.That’s not what Rafat was describing in our conversation. The calm that actually wins is the kind you earn, the kind that comes from knowing what you’re good at, having done the work enough times to trust your own informed point-of-view, and no longer needing to prove any of it to anyone.ADP’s global study found that the workers using AI the most heavily reported significantly less stress than the ones barely touching it, about half as many said they felt overloaded.Ethan Mollick has been saying for years that the people who get their hands on AI, who learn its edges and its failures firsthand, are the ones who stop fearing it and start using it well.Familiarity is what turns a vague threat into a known quantity. The dread lives in the gap between you and the thing you’re afraid of.Patrick Neeman argues that the way out of AI anxiety is to trade the vague fear, the sense that you’re falling behind because everyone else seems to get it, for a specific picture of what would actually have to change in how you work. Vague is the natural state of panic. Specific is the natural state of calm.The discomfort of being visibly bad at something new, Neeman writes, is just the cost of staying in the game.This is where Rafat Ali’s point-of-view comes back in, because it turns out his advice wasn’t a passing mood. Ali actually built his whole company around it. When he relaunched Skift in September 2026, he wrote that AI is making information cheaper every month and judgment more valuable, and the three things that never get cheaper are knowledge nobody else has, a point of view on what it means, and access to the people who make the decisions.The calm he promised me and the strategy he bet his company on are the same thing. Both come from being secure in the one thing the machine can’t hand you.In a moment when no one is sure what’s happening, the calm, informed person doesn’t just steady themselves, they become the one everyone else steadies against. That is the oldest definition of leadership there is.The reason panic is such a bad trade is that it spends all your energy on the part you can’t control, the speed of the technology, and none on the part you can, the judgment you bring to it.You can either dread the future or help build it.The future is a design problemThere’s a specific cost to the panic that most people miss.Gallup found that when a worker crosses over into believing their job is likely to be eliminated, their engagement drops, their burnout climbs, their satisfaction falls, and they become measurably more likely to start looking for the exit. The belief does the damage, often well before the technology does anything at all.Panic is not a neutral way to wait out a storm. It quietly degrades the exact things, your focus, your judgment, your work, that you’d need to come through it well.The real question is what you do with the uncertainty instead. Economist David Autor argues that the AI future should not be not treated as a prediction exercise, but rather as a design problem,.We tend to talk about what’s coming as though it’s weather, something to forecast and brace for. Autor’s point is that we have enormous say in how it actually goes, through the choices we make and the things we decide to build.The future isn’t something you wait to find out. It’s something you have a hand in making.Economists aren’t the only ones saying this. Carolyn Dewar, who advises chief executives at McKinsey, bluntly says that AI won’t decide the future, the people leading through it will.That’s really a description of what leadership has always been. The best leaders stay calm when no one else does. They get informed instead of getting loud, and they keep making clear-eyed decisions while everyone around them spins out.A moment of maximum uncertainty is exactly when that kind of person becomes most valuable.Panic is abdication. Calm, informed, and decisive drives success.That is the difference between panic and calm. One treats the future as weather, something you brace for and can’t change. The other treats it as a problem, which is a thing you already know how to handle.Which brings me back to Rafat Ali and to the thing he told me about turning 50. The relief he promised was finally putting away the weight of trying to prove you belong, and discovering that what’s left underneath is everything you actually know how to do. That’s the same calm that wins right now, the calm of someone who has stopped bracing for the future and started building their small corner of it.You can spend this moment frightened of what AI might take from you or you can get quiet, take stock of what you actually bring, and go to work.The people who come through this just fine are already doing the second thing. They put the panic down, and they got back to the part that was always theirs.References and further readingThe fear is realPew Research Center, Americans Are Increasingly Wary of AI. The survey finding that 71 percent of Americans expect AI to mean fewer jobs over the next twenty years, rising to 73 percent among adults under 30.Nela Richardson and ADP Research, Today at Work. A global study of more than thirty-nine thousand workers finding that anxiety, not confidence, now defines how people feel about their jobs.Sylvia Brafman Mental Health Center, The AI Anxiety Era. A survey finding nearly half of workers say AI worry has hurt their mental health, climbing to two in three among the youngest.Dr. Simbiat Adighije, Anticipatory Anxiety About AI Is Showing Up in Clinic (KevinMD). A psychiatrist on treating patients for AI dread, and why the anxiety is real whether or not the prediction driving it comes true.Zachary Sikora, 5 Things You Never Knew About Fear (Northwestern Medicine). On fear as a survival response, and how it impairs the brain’s reasoning and judgment when it spikes.We have seen this panic beforeDora Czerna, Disruption Has a Shape. A designer tracing the recurring arc of technological disruption, democratization, panic, quality collapse, then new norms.Calestous Juma, Why Do People Resist New Technologies? (World Economic Forum). A Harvard professor on six hundred years of fear and resistance to new technology, from coffee to electricity.Derek Thompson, Why America’s AI Discourse Feels So Broken. On history as the strongest argument that AI won’t cause an overnight jobs apocalypse.Nancy Koehn, Leadership Under Pressure (Harvard Business School). On research showing most leaders turn closed-minded and reactive in a crisis, and why the steady ones are rare.The calm that wins is earnedEthan Mollick, Doing Stuff with AI (One Useful Thing). On why the people who get their hands on AI, and learn its edges firsthand, stop fearing it and start using it well.Patrick Neeman, AI Wants Builders. On trading the vague fear of falling behind for a specific picture of what would actually have to change in how you work.Rafat Ali, The New Skift. The Skift founder’s argument that AI makes information cheaper and judgment more valuable, and that knowledge, a point of view, and access never get cheaper.The future is a design problemVibhas Ratanjee and Gallup, Your Most AI-Fluent Employees Are the Most Afraid. On how believing your job will be eliminated measurably drops engagement and raises burnout, often before the technology does anything.David Autor, on treating the AI future as a design problem rather than a prediction exercise, and the enormous say we have in how it actually goes.Carolyn Dewar, AI Won’t Decide the Future. Leaders Will (McKinsey, via Fortune). On judgment as the thing that can’t be outsourced, and leadership as the work of staying clear-eyed under uncertainty.In a world of panic, calm and certainty win was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: AI can generate the interface. What makes it worth caring about?
item.description: As more product work is generated from shared patterns, designers need to decide where an experience should surprise, celebrate, or simply leave someone alone.Imagine asking an AI tool to design a task-completion state.The result has a checkmark, a friendly message, and a small burst of confetti. It uses the right components. The spacing matches the system. The animation is polished.Now imagine that same response after two different tasks.In one, someone has finished setting up a business they have spent months trying to launch. In the other, an administrator has updated the forty-seventh record of the morning.The component is consistent. The experiences should probably be different.Nothing in the confetti explains which moment deserves it. That decision depends on what the person has done, how often they do it, and whether they want the product to make an occasion of it.As AI becomes more capable of assembling interfaces from established patterns, this distinction deserves more attention. We are getting better at telling tools what belongs to our product. We also need to decide what belongs to the moment.Different moments call for different levels of acknowledgment. Zillow’s success-state starter kit makes room for both quiet confirmation and celebration. Image credit: Kudzai Chinyadza, Celebratory Success States.Matching the system is an incomplete definition of qualityThere are good reasons to care about consistency. People should not have to relearn familiar actions on every screen. Teams should not spend their time reconstructing decisions already made elsewhere.Figma’s guidance on working with its agent describes how components, guidelines, examples, and task-specific context help generated work reflect a team’s product. That is useful progress. It also makes clear that consistency depends on the context supplied to the tool.But a faithful rendering of a system can still be an emotionally inappropriate response.A success message can be correct and patronizing. An illustration can match the brand and occupy space someone needs for their work. A playful loading state can be charming until it appears during a time-sensitive task.These failures are difficult to identify by inspecting the component alone. They emerge from the relationship between the component and the person encountering it.In my earlier article about design-system judgment, I explored the distinction between enforcing rules and deciding whether a pattern is appropriate. Expression brings another version of that problem into view: a detail can follow every rule we wrote and still misunderstand the occasion.I want software to have room for color, humor, beauty, and small surprises.I want an interaction to feel satisfying, even when satisfaction cannot be reduced to a shorter completion time.I also want the product to recognize when I have work to do.Pleasure has a history beyond the AI conversationDesigners were studying this long before generative interfaces.Don Norman’s work on emotional design considers appearance, the experience of using something, and the meaning people attach to it. That gives us a broader vocabulary than “add delight.” Pleasure can come from how something looks, how well it responds, or what owning and using it means to someone.Therese Fessenden’s distinction between surface and deep delight is useful here too. An amusing detail can create a moment of pleasure, while a well-considered workflow can produce a quieter satisfaction that lasts through the task.The second does not make the first disposable.A product can be dependable and exuberant. A useful tool can have a peculiar illustration or a lovely transition simply because someone cared about making it enjoyable. We do not have to defend every expressive choice by pretending it saves three seconds.But we do have to understand what it asks of the person.A color choice might make a screen more inviting without adding a step. A celebration might demand attention. A joke might require cultural familiarity. A transition might make a relationship easier to understand — or force someone to wait.“Delight” is too generous a label to apply before finding out which of those things happened.A playful product still needs restraintDuolingo offers an instructive example because expression is already central to its identity.In its account of redesigning the app’s core tabs, the team describes experimenting with several visual directions, then finding tensions between consistency and purpose. An illustrated header on every tab created uniformity, but some illustrations occupied space without communicating anything useful.The solution included different header sizes for different purposes, with titles kept in consistent positions.That is a more useful lesson than “make every screen playful.” A recognizable product can vary its emphasis while preserving familiar structure. The team’s own account shows that even an expressive brand needs to ask where an illustration earns its space.Credit: DuolingoThis matters when a design becomes an example for AI to reuse.If the reference screen has a large illustration, should the next screen have one too? Is the illustration a general rule, a possibility, or a response to a particular situation?A tool can reproduce the visible answer while missing the reason for it. So can a designer working from an incomplete specification.As generation becomes easier, that missing explanation can travel further. A choice made for one meaningful moment becomes the default for several ordinary ones.The expressive detail survives. Its purpose does not.Consistency can include a change in toneMailchimp’s voice-and-tone guidance makes an important distinction: its voice remains recognizable, while its tone responds to the reader’s circumstances.The guide welcomes humor but gives clarity priority. It asks writers to consider whether someone has finished a campaign or is confused and looking for help, and warns against forcing a joke.This is a practical way to preserve personality without requiring the same emotional performance everywhere.Credit: MailchimpA product’s identity can live in how sensitively it changes.Warmth during onboarding might mean encouragement. Warmth after an error might mean a direct explanation, preserved work, and a clear next step. The writing can sound like the same company without treating both situations as opportunities for comedy.That distinction should also shape instructions given to AI.“Make it friendly and playful” leaves a great deal unresolved. Friendly to whom? Playful at what point? What has just happened?A more useful instruction describes the situation: the user’s work is safe; they need to understand why the action failed; avoid humor; make the recovery path obvious.There is still room for good writing within those constraints. The constraints establish what the writing owes the person.Expression can make an interface clearerIt is tempting to organize this debate as a negotiation between expressive design and usable design. Google’s research on Material 3 Expressive complicates that framing.In its published research account, Google describes an email interface where the Send button became larger, more prominent, and closer to the keyboard. Participants located it faster. The expressive treatment also changed hierarchy and placement; its benefit cannot be attributed to decoration alone.The same report includes a less successful experiment: a playlist replaced familiar rows with a scattered arrangement of album artwork. Participants found it visually exciting, but usability suffered.These are findings from Google’s tested designs, not evidence that every product should adopt the same aesthetic. Together, they show why the actual interaction matters more than the adjective attached to it.Credit: Google DesignColor can establish emphasis. Shape can distinguish actions. Motion can show where something went. An expressive decision may help people understand a product while making it more pleasurable.The question is what remains legible after we introduce it.A familiar control can carry considerable character. A surprising arrangement can remove the very cues someone needs to use it. Designers have to examine both effects, rather than accepting “on brand” or “more delightful” as sufficient explanations.The same delight can become someone else’s interruptionAsana’s celebrations show why preference belongs in this discussion.Its 2016 introduction of an expanded celebration system described occasional animated characters appearing after task completion, with celebrations enabled through settings.A 2018 community discussion captures the other side: a customer found the characters intrusive and asked how to disable them. A reply explained the setting.That exchange does not establish how most users felt. It does show that the same detail can be welcome to one person and unwelcome to another.Credit: AsanaThis is where the word “delight” can hide an assumption. We describe our intention as though it were already the user’s response.A celebration designed to recognize accomplishment may become an obstacle during repetitive work. Something enjoyed privately may feel inappropriate during a presentation. Someone may like the character and still prefer to finish without watching it.Giving people control is part of designing the experience well.For motion, the stakes can extend beyond preference. W3C’s guidance for Animation from Interactions, a Level AAA criterion, explains why people need ways to disable nonessential interaction-triggered movement, including the potential for vestibular symptoms.An expressive experience should have a considered reduced-motion version. Removing movement should leave clear feedback, meaningful hierarchy, and an understandable result.There are many ways to make something feel good. Movement is one of them.AI changes how easily the wrong detail can spreadNone of these problems began with AI. Teams have copied patterns without understanding them for years.What AI introduces is another way to reproduce those decisions — and an opportunity to be more explicit about them.A library might describe a celebration’s colors, duration, and animation curve. That describes the asset. It says little about whether a celebration should happen after someone completes a tutorial, pays a bill, or removes an account.Those are different events even if the system labels all three “success.”Here is a hypothetical rule worth testing: a fuller acknowledgment for a meaningful first achievement; brief feedback for repeated routine actions; direct, restrained language for sensitive outcomes.That rule will not fit every product. Its value is that it gives the team something concrete to question.Is the first achievement actually meaningful to the person, or merely valuable to our onboarding metrics? Does a repeated action become meaningful when it completes a larger goal? Are we assuming we know how someone feels because we know which button they pressed?A good specification should leave those questions visible.AI can help explore expressive alternatives: different copy, motion treatments, layouts, and levels of emphasis. There is no need to claim that surprise or beauty belongs exclusively to human production.But producing an alternative and establishing when it is welcome are different kinds of work.If we evaluate generated interfaces mainly by how closely they match the library, we will favor what is easiest to compare. If we ask whether the experience suits the occasion, we need examples, use over time, and feedback from the people living with it.That is a broader evaluation than a screenshot review can provide.“Worth caring about” should not mean harder to leaveThere is another complication: products can use expression to serve goals people did not choose.A cheerful character might encourage a useful habit. It might also make declining an offer feel like disappointing someone. A reward animation might acknowledge progress, or distract from how little progress actually occurred.Those possibilities need to remain in the argument. Emotional design is capable of persuasion as well as pleasure.The appropriate question is whose purpose the detail advances.Does it help someone enjoy an activity they value? Does it acknowledge something they accomplished? Or does it make the product’s preferred behavior harder to refuse?Time spent and repeat visits cannot answer that on their own. Someone may return because the product is useful, because leaving is costly, or because a mechanic creates pressure. Those explanations have different implications for design.I am interested in software people appreciate using. That requires taking their ability to dislike a detail seriously, even when it is the detail the team loves most.Give the expressive decision a proper reviewIn a product team, this work needs a place before the final polish pass.For a proposed expressive moment, I would want to see it in three conditions: the first encounter, repeated use, and a situation where the person is rushed or something has gone wrong.The same animation may behave beautifully in isolation and become tiring in a sequence. The same line of copy may be reassuring on a quiet afternoon and dismissive during a failure.Research should make room for those differences. Watch whether people can continue. Ask what they think the response means. Find out whether they want to see it again. Include people who prefer less motion or sound, and test whether the experience still communicates clearly.These observations will not produce a universal delight score. They can help us distinguish a detail people value from one they tolerate.This also changes what we document.Alongside the approved example, record the circumstance it serves, when to scale it back, and a case where it should not be used. Give both people and AI tools a reason to choose differently.A design system can document when to hold back. Adobe Spectrum recommends restrained illustrations for errors, where an upbeat visual can clash with the user’s situation. Image credit: Adobe Spectrum, Illustration guidelines.A system with that kind of guidance can protect character. It can make room for an unusual illustration, a distinctive rhythm, or a moment of celebration while keeping everyday work dependable.The alternative is to encode only what is easy to repeat and hope the rest survives delivery.I want the products we build with AI to have more room for pleasure: a color choice that lifts a screen, a response that acknowledges effort, a transition that feels unusually right. I also want that pleasure to survive actual use, beyond the first demo and the designer’s own preferences.Return to the two completed tasks. The new business owner and the administrator may both need confirmation. One might welcome a moment to take in what they have accomplished. The other might want the next record ready.AI can generate both responses.We still have to notice that the occasions are different.AI can generate the interface. What makes it worth caring about? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: What AI has changed in Design Systems, and what is still up to us
item.description: Three design experts told me how AI is changing the way we build and maintain Design Systems. And led me to think that “the future” is already happening now.What is the human role in creating and maintaining a design system in the AI era? Credit: Anna Lefour with Gemini.You’ve probably read, or even written, one of those LinkedIn posts about someone building a complete Design System in 20 minutes with Claude. Or in 15 minutes with Gemini. Or… you get the idea.Those posts made me curious. I had never built a full Design System, although I had set up the basic elements of one before I really dug into AI, and it was as interesting as it was painful. So the promise of building a full one in minutes was appealing.My mistake? Confusing a UI kit with a Design System, and believing the whole process could really be done in minutes.At UXDX Berlin last May, two talks about Design Systems made me want to know more about how AI has changed them in the day-to-day of product teams. That curiosity led me to interview three design experts, and to get to the essential part of what a Design System actually is: Marianne Ashton-Booth, Head of Product Design at ITV; David Sward, Chief Design Officer at Siemens; and Nicolas Chatelain, freelance Senior Designer and specialized in Design System and Ops.Three experts, three different approaches. Nicolas Chatelain bets on a frame that bends without breaking, flexible with teams and ready for AI. David Sward bets on speed with guardrails, with AI as a tool and a human in the loop. Marianne Ashton-Booth bets on people and process, treating the Design System like a product.The last two had both just given a talk at UXDX when I talked with them, so what follows draws on two different moments with each of them: what they said on stage, and what they told me one-on-one afterwards.1. AI automates the easy part, but the hard part still belongs to humansOne-on-one after her talk, Marianne Ashton-Booth said something that felt particularly on point to me: “Anybody can spin up prototypes in minutes, and that’s great. But then that gap between what’s actually feasible, what’s actually close to the brand, or close to the actual components that we’ve got, can be quite distant.”Marianne Ashton-Booth, Head of Product Design at ITV, on the stage of UXDX Berlin last May. Source: UXDX.Nicolas Chatelain, whom I interviewed in July, put the same idea in other words: the UI is the easy part of a Design System. “The hardest part, the one that makes a DS work or not, is governance and adoption.”Neither of them sees the components as the problem; Nicolas even says anyone could, indeed, build a kit while we were talking. What matters is consistency across teams, and across a whole company, and that is the human part of a Design System. A Zeroheight report on the state of Design Systems, published in early 2026, points the same way: 59% of practitioners credit communication and community for their system’s adoption.On stage, Marianne Ashton-Booth had already named what breaks instead. When a design system fails, she said, “it’s almost never just [the design system’s core operations]. The components are usually fine.” What breaks are the invisible layers underneath: trust, communication, prioritisation, relationships, and shared belief.2. The bottleneck has moved from production speed to review“My biggest problem is trying to slow people down with AI,” David Sward told me. Indeed, AI has sped up a lot of processes, all the way to delivery.Here, he does not mean slowing his team down so that they get used to AI, but keeping them inside the security and compliance rules of a large enterprise. With hundreds of products relying on his system, a mistake would take several hundred million euros to fix. His operating principle: “don’t break things.”But the fact remains: productivity has risen. And once speed is there, the bottleneck shifts from production to the people who review, validate and keep everything coherent. Nicolas Chatelain and Marianne Ashton-Booth ran into this too.During Nicolas Chatelain’s mission for an international group, for example, AI-boosted product teams started to outpace the central Design System team, whose original strategy was to lock everything down. His verdict:“With AI, it’s a total rollback. We have to become much more flexible, because tomorrow people could create a kit in five minutes. If we become useless, they’ll find an even easier way to bypass us.”Figma’s slots, which let teams put their own content inside a standardised component, are one way to loosen the frame.At ITV, Marianne Ashton-Booth’s team takes another route and relies on “design system reps” in both design and engineering: “They tend to be the go-to people that have a little bit more prominence and involvement in things like final decisions. It just means that things can keep moving rather than just becoming a bit of a bottleneck.” On stage, she added that rather than treating AI as a separate topic, ITV asked the right question: “What does that mean for the design system? How should our processes evolve?”These three approaches suggest that there is no single way to handle the bottleneck: it depends on the context, the level of risk, and how far AI has advanced, and been accepted, in the organisation. That is precisely where humans remain useful: understanding at what moment, and to what extent, everyone who holds decision-making power over the Design System should step in, and when they should let go.3. The Design System is becoming something AI readsThis is the part that sounds most like “the future”, but is actually already the present: making the system readable for machines.Nicolas Chatelain’s team started watching tools like V0 and Lovable in the second half of 2025, and concluded it was too early to adopt them. They chose to prepare the system instead: tokens migrated to the DTCG (Design Tokens Community Group) standard, a shared format for the values of a system, like colours, spacing or typography, so that every tool, and every AI agent, reads them the same way.This extract of Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent’s report shows the capabilities of the systems he analysedAn MCP server (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI agent query the Design System directly, for instance to find the right component or token, instead of guessing. In a field study published in July 2026, Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent looked at 21 open-source Design Systems: 20 of them offer an MCP server (official or community-built), but only 3 have set up Figma Code Connect, which ties a Figma component to its real code counterpart. Plenty of systems let AI read them, far fewer tie their components back to design.David Sward’s team uses AI on the other side of the process: a large language model (LLM) compares what teams have implemented with what the Design System is supposed to be, and, in his words, “systematically tells you what to fix.” In his own Design System, AI stays “a tool just like anything else” (an engine harmonises thousands of icons, for instance), and his broader principle holds: “You can’t remove a human from the loop and then expect them to step back in to operate the system if they don’t understand the state the system is in.”Marianne Ashton-Booth, on her end, is adamant: “There might be parts of [a design system] that become more AI-generated or automated. But a design system isn’t just that part, you know, it’s the people and it’s the process as well. And that’s the bit that I think we’ll still retain.”Where I think we’re heading: code as the source of truthThese insights led me to believe this is where Design Systems are heading: the code, rather than the design file, is becoming their source of truth. We might already be there. Designers who use AI seem to open Figma less and less (that’s my case), and in teams where shipping and iterating beat perfecting details, the blurring of roles (I talked about it here) doesn’t help.Nicolas Chatelain said it: “Today, the source of truth has to be the code. Absolutely.” Working in the code removes a layer of abstraction between AI and production, and “tomorrow, when this documentation lives directly in the code, we won’t need Figma anymore.” He admits he may be “completely wrong”, and still finds Figma useful to explore and fine-tune. And I agree with him that Figma isn’t dead. But for me its place in the process has definitely changed.Concretely, it means that whatever is merged into the code becomes the standard, and design files, documentation and AI agents all read from it. Every review then becomes a governance decision. But as Tony Ward wrote in his recent article “Code as the Source of Truth”, the key is to keep “a subject-matter expert in the loop at every step of the way.” Which leaves the real question: in this new process, who gets to say what goes into the truth?As for me, meeting these three experts showed me there is no single answer to that question. Each built theirs from their own environment, and in that richness I found keys to meet my own challenges. I hope you will too.Thanks to UXDX for providing access to the event, and to David Sward, Marianne Ashton-Booth and Nicolas Chatelain for their time.All of Nicolas Chatelain’s quotes were translated from French.What AI has changed in Design Systems, and what is still up to us was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Everyone is building AI agents. Who’s designing the stop button?
item.description: We used to design predictable user flows. Now AI can interpret, decide, and act on its own. Here’s why the hardest design decisions happen where that autonomy ends.Showing where AI stops in the flow — by gptIn September 2025, researchers at Thinking Machines Lab ran the same prompt through a language model 1,000 times. They set the temperature to zero, a setting that should, in theory, make token selection deterministic.They got 80 different completions from the same prompt, model, and settings.What’s even more interesting is that all 1,000 outputs were identical for the first 102 tokens. The differences started at token 103, when the model described where Richard Feynman was born.The researchers traced the variation to how computations were performed under different server batching conditions. With a modified implementation, they eventually got all 1,000 outputs to match.Their research demonstrated something important. Even when you try to make a language model behave predictably, the infrastructure running it can introduce variation.Now imagine building a product on top of that model. One that creates freight bookings, updates customer records, or moves medical documents between systems.The problem isn’t that AI can produce different answers. That’s often exactly why we’re using it.The problem starts when those answers turn into actions, and nobody has decided which parts of the process are allowed to be unpredictable.For decades, we designed software around the assumption that we knew what would happen next. AI is making that assumption increasingly difficult to maintain. And I think a lot of early-stage teams are still designing as if nothing has changed.—We used to know what would happen nextThink about how we’ve designed digital products for the last few decades.You open an app, select something, complete a form, click a button, and move to the next step. The interface responds according to predefined rules.Michal’s project — TIER Energy networkA flight booking is a good example. Select your destination, choose a date, pick a flight, enter passenger details, pay, and receive confirmation.There might be hundreds of conditions behind that experience, but the designer and engineering team can define them in advance. If the payment fails, show an error. If a seat is unavailable, offer another. If information is missing, ask the user to complete it.This is the thinking that shaped most of our design tools and methods. User flows, wireframes, journey maps, information architecture, design systems, and interactive prototypes.We design states and transitions between them. We decide what happens when someone clicks a button, makes a mistake, or returns to an unfinished process.Traditional software was never perfectly deterministic. Search results changed, recommendations were personalized, and external services could fail. But the core behavior of most transactional interfaces was defined by explicit rules.The designer didn’t need to know which flight someone would book. They needed to know how booking a flight worked.What’s interesting is that the idea of software moving beyond explicit commands is not new. In 1993, Jakob Nielsen wrote about noncommand user interfaces. He described systems that could infer what users wanted instead of requiring them to communicate everything through specific commands. That was more than 30 years ago.We’ve been imagining software that understands intention for decades. We just couldn’t build many of those experiences in a commercially practical way.Now we can and that changes what it means to design a user flow.—The user no longer has to define every stepImagine you’re designing a reporting tool.Previously, a user would select data, configure filters, choose a report format, generate the report, and download it. The interface existed to collect instructions.Classic vs AI flow — by gptToday, someone can simply write: “Tell me why our conversion dropped last month and what we should investigate.”The product can interpret the request, retrieve information, compare periods, identify patterns, and decide how to present the findings.We removed five steps from the interface, but we introduced a completely different kind of complexity.What if the data is incomplete? What if two dashboards define conversion differently? What if the AI produces a convincing explanation that is actually incorrect?A traditional user flow doesn’t fully capture these possibilities because the system can now make decisions about how to approach the task.This is also where the difference between AI adoption and actual automation becomes interesting.According to the 2026 Stanford AI Index, 88% of surveyed organizations reported using AI in 2025, up from 55% in 2023. Yet scaled AI agent deployment remained in the single digits across nearly all business functions.Companies are using AI, but letting it run meaningful business processes is a very different challenge.There’s a big difference between asking AI to draft an email and allowing it to send that email to 4,000 customers.This is where UX becomes much more important than simply making the interface look intelligent.—Non-deterministic vs deterministicI think it’s worth clarifying the terminology because we tend to mix these things together.A deterministic system follows predefined logic. Given the same relevant input and state, the same rules produce the same output.A non-deterministic system can produce different outcomes under apparently identical conditions. With generative AI, it’s often more useful to talk about probabilistic behavior, interpretation, and uncertainty.Think about the difference between validating an email address and understanding what an email means.Checking whether an email address has the correct format is a deterministic task.Understanding whether an incoming message is a complaint, a booking request, or a pricing enquiry requires interpretation.Now connect that interpretation to an actual workflow.If the AI decides it’s a booking request, it might create a shipment. If it decides it’s a complaint, it might escalate the issue. If it identifies a pricing enquiry, it might prepare a quotation.The user didn’t explicitly select a workflow. The system did.So yes, the output might be non-deterministic UI. The wording changes, the content changes, and sometimes even the structure of what appears on the screen changes.But the bigger problem is UX.Users need to understand what the system is doing, predict the consequences of their actions, correct mistakes, and know when they can trust an outcome.You can design a beautiful AI interface with great typography, smooth animations, and perfectly polished chat components. But if the underlying system makes decisions users cannot understand or correct, the experience is broken.The difficult part is designing what the product is allowed to do with that response.—The biggest mistake is making everything non-deterministicThere’s an assumption that the more autonomous an AI product becomes, the better it is.Why ask people to complete forms when AI can understand them? Why use predefined workflows when an agent can decide what to do?Those are reasonable questions. But just because AI can interpret information doesn’t mean it should be responsible for executing every resulting action.And just because a product uses AI doesn’t mean everything inside it has to behave probabilistically.In fact, some of the more interesting AI products are doing the opposite. They’re deliberately combining deterministic and non-deterministic systems, deciding exactly where each one should take control.A lot of failures come from making something non-deterministic that should have been a form.This is especially relevant for early-stage founders. It’s tempting to turn every interaction into a prompt because it makes the product feel more advanced.But sometimes a form, a predefined workflow, or a simple confirmation button is exactly what the experience needs.Two products illustrate this particularly well.—Routine Labs: Let AI build the workflow, not improvise while running itRoutine Labs works on automating processes inside existing legacy software, particularly in healthcare. Its approach is interesting because AI is used to help build automations, while production execution follows deterministic workflows.Imagine a medical practice dealing with documents across several applications. A blood test arrives and needs to be identified, checked against patient consent, and uploaded to Germany’s electronic patient record, known as the ePA.Traditionally, someone has to move between systems, find the correct information, check the necessary conditions, and complete the process manually.A fully autonomous AI agent could attempt to interpret and navigate that process every time.Routine takes a different approach.According to the company, its hybrid engine uses generative AI to create automations, but the workflows running in production follow repeatable, logged logic. On its healthcare website, Routine also states that it doesn’t use AI during production operations or transfer personal data to LLMs.Routine Labs — by gptThat’s a very deliberate product decision. The uncertainty is concentrated in building the automation, where the process can be defined and checked. Production execution is designed to be predictable.Now think about what that means for UX.The user doesn’t necessarily need a conversation with an agent. They need to know what automation is running, which steps have been completed, whether the correct document was processed, and whether something requires their attention.Routine’s public product examples show exactly this type of workflow: search for blood tests, check ePA consent, and upload the document.The interface can communicate progress and exceptions through familiar patterns such as status indicators, execution histories, and review steps. No chatbot required.And that’s what makes this approach interesting. The intelligence is used where it adds value, without making the entire experience dependent on the model interpreting the process correctly every single time.Routine is an example of how you can build an AI-native product while keeping its actual execution deterministic.—Zauber: Let AI handle ambiguity, but make uncertainty visibleZauber approaches the same problem from a different direction.It builds AI agents for sea and air freight forwarding, working inside existing tools such as Outlook and integrating with systems like CargoWise.Freight forwarding is an interesting environment for AI because so much operational work depends on interpreting unstructured information.Emails, PDFs, packing lists, changing shipment details, special instructions, and incomplete documents. Information comes from different sources and doesn’t always agree.An operator might receive an email requesting a shipment booking, with a packing list attached and a delivery date changed somewhere in the conversation.Traditionally, someone would read everything, interpret the request, check the details, and manually enter the information into the booking system.Zauber uses AI to handle much of that interpretation.Its agents can read rate requests, identify relevant shipment details, retrieve rates, and prepare quotations for review. For booking creation, they can extract information from emails and documents and populate the necessary fields in CargoWise.But the most interesting part is how the product handles information it cannot verify.According to Zauber’s product page, if a declared value is missing or the volume doesn’t match the packing list, the system flags the discrepancy rather than guessing. The operator confirms the information before the booking is created.Zauber visualized — by gptImagine the email says a shipment has a volume of 58.4 m³, while the packing list says 60.03 m³.The AI has already completed most of the work, but the interface should make that disagreement visible, show where the information came from, and let the operator resolve it.Instead of asking the user to complete every field, the product directs their attention to the two fields that matter. That’s a different way of designing workflows.And there’s another detail I like about Zauber. Its product documentation describes monitoring agent sessions, including where the workflow hands control back to a human operator. The handover itself becomes something the company can observe, measure, and improve.Routine and Zauber use different architectures, but they make a similar decision. They don’t treat autonomy as an all-or-nothing feature.Creating a draft based on query: source: gozauber.comThey decide where the AI should interpret information, where deterministic rules should take over, and when the user needs to step in.—Why a great AI demo can become a terrible productHere’s a simple calculation that explains why these decisions matter.Imagine a workflow with ten steps. Each step has a 95% chance of completing correctly, and all ten steps must succeed. Assuming the outcomes are independent, the probability of the entire workflow succeeding is:0.⁹⁵¹⁰ = 59.9% by gpt.A workflow that’s 95% reliable at each individual step could succeed end to end only about 60% of the time.This is a simplified example, not a measured AI failure rate. Real systems have dependencies, validation, retries, and recovery mechanisms that change the result. But it illustrates why model accuracy alone isn’t a sufficient product metric.An AI might extract information correctly most of the time. What happens when it doesn’t? What if an incorrect value gets passed to another system? What if an action succeeds but the confirmation fails? What happens if the agent repeats the action and creates a duplicate?A lot of products look great because we’ve designed and tested the successful version.The first time the model gets confused, the actual product experience begins. That’s where traditional design tools start showing their limitations.A Figma prototype is excellent for representing predefined states. It’s not particularly good at representing a distribution of possible outputs, variable execution paths, or a failure that happens once in 50 runs.This doesn’t make Figma irrelevant. It means static screens are no longer enough to validate the behavior we’re designing.—What happens when we ignore this?One common failure is the illusion of completion.An agent says it updated a record, sent an email, or created a booking. But perhaps it only prepared the action. Maybe an API failed. Maybe the system saved the wrong information.If the interface displays the model’s response as proof that the action succeeded, the user has no reliable way to know what happened.My own resourcesAnother is hidden uncertainty. Information extracted from a document might appear exactly like verified information retrieved from a database. The interface gives both the same visual weight, even though one is an interpretation and the other is an authoritative value.My own resourcesThen there’s the opposite problem: excessive human supervision.Some products solve uncertainty by asking users to approve absolutely everything. But if someone has to review 100 decisions and 98 are consistently correct, they eventually stop paying attention.You’ve automated the original work and replaced it with a new job: supervising the automation.My own resourcesThat’s not necessarily a better product.There’s also the problem of incorrect decisions spreading through otherwise reliable systems. An AI might identify the wrong customer, after which every deterministic step executes perfectly while updating the wrong records.The system worked exactly as designed, but the business outcome was wrong.It takes us to the point when designing error states isn’t enough. We need to design the relationship between interpretation, verification, execution, and recovery.—How I approach designing this in an early-stage teamWorking on a new AI product today, I’d start by mapping the workflow into three categories: deterministic, fuzzy, and irreversible.It’s a simple exercise, but it forces you to make decisions that are easy to ignore when you’re focused on the demo.Deterministic steps are operations with clear rules. Validating required fields, checking permissions, retrieving records, and preventing duplicate actions. These should generally be handled through conventional software.Fuzzy steps require interpretation. Reading an email, understanding a document, classifying a request, or drafting a response. This is where AI becomes useful.Irreversible or high-impact steps are actions with meaningful consequences. Sending an external email, issuing a payment, changing a sensitive record, or committing a booking. These need explicit permission boundaries, verification, and, where appropriate, human approval.Deterministic, Fuzzy, and Irreversible steps — by chat gptOnce you’ve mapped those steps, a lot of product decisions become clearer. You can decide where the model is actually needed, what the interface needs to communicate, and which actions should never happen silently.The next thing I’d do is stop treating the AI output as the interface itself. For many B2B products, I’d rather have the model return structured information and let deterministic components render it.If an agent extracts booking information, the user should see a normal booking interface, not a paragraph explaining what the model found. The model fills in the card. It doesn’t need to invent the card.Let’s take something everyone understands. Booking a flight.You ask an AI assistant to book an early flight to Lisbon on Friday for you and Ania, returning Sunday evening.First, the fuzzy part. The model has to interpret what “early” and “evening” mean, figure out which Ania you’re talking about, and make a few assumptions based on your previous bookings.Instead of giving you a long chat response, the UI presents a structured draft. You can see what the model understood, where each assumption came from, and correct anything that looks wrong. Nothing has been booked yet.My own resourcesThen comes deterministic validation. The system checks actual flight availability, passenger details, fare conditions, and prices against the airline’s data and predefined rules.Everything checks out. Two seats are available, the refundable fare costs €398, and it’s within your budget. The interface shows a verified booking summary, without making you go through every individual check.My own resourcesNow the interesting part.You click Book, but the refundable fare sells out before the booking is completed. The only remaining option is €342, but it’s non-refundable.Technically, it’s cheaper. It even passes your budget limit. But it’s not what you originally agreed to.This is where the interface needs to change. Instead of letting the agent choose the cheaper ticket, the UI explains what happened, keeps all the information that’s still valid, and asks whether you want to book the non-refundable fare or look for another option.My own resourcesLooking at the entire flow, the interesting part is how the boundaries change. The model can interpret the request, but it can’t set prices or book anything. Rules and live systems handle validation. And when the refundable fare suddenly becomes unavailable, the system stops and hands the decision back to the user.Here’s how those boundaries work across the same booking:My own resourcesOne booking, three different levels of autonomy. The system can interpret, validate, and prepare actions, but the rules for handing control back to the user change depending on the consequences.This is why I don’t think we can design AI workflows as just a sequence of predetermined screens anymore.The same task moves between interpretation, validation, and execution. A decision that seemed straightforward a moment ago can suddenly require human judgment.And the interface has to handle that without making someone start the whole process again.There’s no need to show confidence scores or explain every decision the model makes. Show the assumptions when they matter, keep routine checks in the background, and make the consequences clear when something changes.The difficult part is designing the transition between them.—Prototype the behavior, not just the happy pathI’d also move to working prototypes earlier.Tools like Cursor, Lovable, v0, and Claude Code make it easier to build interfaces connected to actual model behavior. You can still start in Figma, but at some point you need to see the variability rather than imagine it.Run the same scenario repeatedly. Try different phrasing. Use incomplete documents. Give the system conflicting instructions. Turn the failures into evaluation cases.Anthropic’s research on building effective agents makes a useful distinction between predefined workflows and agents that dynamically decide their own steps. It also recommends starting with the simplest architecture that can solve the problem.Not everything needs an agent. Sometimes a fixed workflow with one intelligent step is more useful, less expensive, and significantly easier to test.For the actual implementation, structured outputs, schemas, state machines, execution logs, and human approval mechanisms help make these boundaries real. Tools like LangGraph and LangSmith can support stateful workflows, tracing, and evaluation.None of these tools eliminates model uncertainty. They help you design a product that knows what to do when uncertainty appears.Finally, I’d measure something more useful than how often the AI completes a task. I’d measure how much human attention the workflow requires.Things like:How often does someone need to correct the output? How long do those corrections take? How often does the agent require intervention? How many tasks actually finish correctly without creating additional work?An agent that automates 80% of a process but makes the remaining 20% painful may not save much time. The goal is reducing the total effort needed to achieve a reliable outcome.—The hardest decision is how much control to give awayFor founders, this is where UX becomes product strategy.Give AI too little autonomy and you’ve built an expensive assistant that still requires users to do all the work. Give it too much and users have to trust decisions they cannot inspect or predict.My own resourcesThere’s no universal answer because the consequences vary between workflows. Drafting an email is different from sending it. Preparing a booking is different from creating it. Extracting information from a medical document is different from modifying a patient record.And the boundary isn’t necessarily permanent.A workflow might begin with every action requiring approval. After hundreds of successful executions and measurable evidence of reliability, some steps can become automatic. Other steps might always require human involvement because the cost of a mistake is too high.This also changes how I’d approach a zero-to-one product.Instead of promising to automate an entire business operation, I’d start with one painful workflow, make it measurable, understand its exceptions, and gradually expand.“Our AI handles your entire freight operation” might sound impressive.“We turn incoming shipment requests into verified, ready-to-create bookings” is a much clearer product promise.You can measure the time saved. You can understand what goes wrong. You can build trust before introducing more autonomy.And for an early-stage startup, trust is a much more useful asset than an impressive demo.—Design the boundary, not just the flowFor decades, we focused on making software easier for people to navigate. We mapped their journeys, removed unnecessary steps, and made interfaces more predictable.Now we’re increasingly designing software that navigates parts of the work on their behalf. We need to understand what the system knows, what it assumes, what it can verify, and what it’s allowed to do when information is incomplete.We need to decide when the system should act, when it should ask, and when it should stop. And perhaps most importantly, we need to accept that not every part of an AI-native product benefits from more AI.Sometimes the best decision is to let a model interpret something and hand execution to deterministic software. Sometimes it’s to prepare an action and ask for confirmation. Sometimes it’s to admit that there isn’t enough information to continue.Routine Labs and Zauber are useful examples because they make those boundaries part of their product architecture rather than treating them as an afterthought.The next generation of product design isn’t just about making interfaces more intelligent. It’s about deciding how much unpredictability the product can safely absorb.If you’re a founder building in this space, take your most important workflow and mark every step as deterministic, fuzzy, or irreversible. You’ll probably discover more about the product you’re building than you would from another conversation about which AI model to use.Your AI doesn’t need to behave the same way every time. But your users need to know what they can depend on.ReferencesThinking Machines Lab, Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference (2025)Stanford HAI, 2026 AI Index ReportJakob Nielsen, Noncommand User Interfaces (1993)Microsoft Research, Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (2019)Anthropic, Building Effective AgentsRoutine LabsZauber, ProductThe Routine Labs and Zauber examples are based on their publicly available product descriptions, not independent production testing.Everyone is building AI agents. item.title: I let AI build. I don’t let AI decide.
item.description: A long workbench split down the middle, finished tools stacked on one side and a single open notebook on the other.My list of tasks I give models without a second thought and what I review until the tools evolve.I’ve used generative models for almost four years and designed machine learning applications for seven before that, so people ask what I delegate. I approach this as an apologist, someone who makes the case for the technology in the right context.That’s generous, since an OpenAI model declared me dead in 2023.As far as public reports available up to my latest update (October 2024), Patrick Neeman passed away in 2023. So there wouldn’t be 2025 UX activities or updates from him.— GPT-5The reality — I’m a data point of one, and everyone should use their own judgment to make the call, including you.The usual split hands models rote work. Mine doesn’t: I hand over creative first drafts and keep models away from arithmetic and one-way-door analysis.I focus on where the tools are dependable and where my judgment makes the final call.Ethan Mollick showed why the split fails in Centaurs and Cyborgs on the Jagged Frontier (2023). Also, in a Boston Consulting Group experiment, consultants using GPT-4 finished 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with 40% higher quality. Outside the model’s reach, they did worse than people alone.The edge is jagged, so difficulty misleads.My test is the guideline, which is how I build trust in the results. Building work has a guideline outside itself: the page runs or the source checks out.Deciding work writes the guideline and carries my signature.Tasks I Give AIEvery task in this group has a check outside the work, so a wrong answer shows up in minutes. Even here, a human makes the final call.Most of this work doesn’t have to be 100% right, and user experience has always worked that way, AI or not. We never fully know what’s going on in a user’s head, so we design from partial evidence, test, and adjust. A model’s first draft or prototype fits that habit, since it only has to be good enough to react to.The reacting is the craft: educated guesses and judgment calls built on experience, and that taste can never come out of a model. Where it comes from is the subject of How we save entry-level UX work that teaches craft in the time of AI.Research TopicsMarcia J. Bates described searching as berrypicking in The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface (1989). Each result changes the question, and the answer arrives in pieces.This is foundational for how AI works today.I used her ideas to frame search and summarization in legal tech software, and I still research that way.Models make berrypicking faster, surfacing 20 sources while I’d still be reading my third. In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, searching for answers topped the list of tasks respondents now do mostly with artificial intelligence tools, at 54.1%.The model picks berries fast, and I still decide which ones are ripe.The source itself is the guideline: every candidate can be opened and read, so a bad suggestion costs me a minute.The Cognitive Models of Information Retrieval entry on UX Guidelines argues that answers should keep the trail visible. I wrote about the structure underneath that trail in Information architecture is the foundation AI is starving for.Because of this, I write to learn and to codify what I think, so reading the sources is where my thinking takes shape.Generate DraftsMost first drafts I publish now start with a model, written against my style rules, my notes, and an argument I’ve already chosen.A model always needs that context, because a cold prompt gets you the average of the internet, which Scott Jenson called average design. Then I cut, reorder, and send back instructions like “merge and relength” until the piece says what I meant.A draft has a guideline once the argument and the rules exist, and a script grades it against the rule file before I do.The thesis stays mine, because a thesis has no guideline; it is the guideline.A draft is cheap to replace, which frees me to treat the first one as raw material.Because the draft carries my context, it makes me faster.In Study finds ChatGPT boosts worker productivity for some writing tasks, MIT researchers reported that 453 professionals using ChatGPT in 2023 finished writing tasks 40% faster, with work rated 18% higher in quality.What I like most is the surprise: a draft sometimes raises an angle I hadn’t thought of, and the best ones make the final piece.Build PrototypesI’ve always written code, from Perl sites and blogging software to the small tools I build now. Claude Code and Cursor write most of the code behind the Chrome extensions I ship at Extend Chrome and the icon reference at UX Icons.I describe the behavior, read the diff, and click through the result. The browser enforces the guideline: a button either does what I asked or fails in plain view.A prototype asks me to click, which beats trusting the model’s account of its own work.Figma’s 2026 AI report found that the share of designers participating in development nearly doubled in a year, from 21% to 41%. What I hand over is the typing.What the extension should do, and when it’s good enough to publish, stays with me.Automate Repeat WorkAnything I do three times becomes a skill.Anthropic describes skills in Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills as folders of instructions, scripts, and resources an agent loads when a task calls for them. I’ve written them for site uploads, release notes, and the CARE prompt behind this article.Here the last good run is the guideline, since I can see which written step slipped.Aviation learned this early and has refined it ever since.In The Checklist, Walter J. Boyne recounts how the Boeing Model 299 crashed in 1935 with an experienced crew after its controls were left locked, and the Air Corps answered with checklists because the limit was human memory.Counting is its own trap: Mollick notes that a model writes a fine sonnet but misses an exact 50-word poem, because it works in tokens.Don’t ask a model to count. Ask it to write the thing that counts in a deterministic manner.So a model wrote the script that checks every draft for word counts, banned words, and repeated phrases, and I wrote every rule it enforces.Unlike a paper checklist, a skill can improve itself: my research and writing skills fold each correction back into their rules, and new rules wait for my approval.Tasks I Keep Human in the LoopThese are 100% problems, and they’re the reason self-driving cars scare me, because it’s not just about the AI but about the humans around it.A car that handles 99% of the road still meets the last 1% at road speed, with no undo. Some tasks are risky because other humans are involved, each making a judgment call no model can see inside. In 2018, an Uber test vehicle killed Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona, and CNN’s report on the Uber test driver’s 2023 guilty plea notes the safety driver had looked away for more than a third of the trip.Before I’d hand any of these over, two conditions would have to hold:Human in the loop: Review the work before it takes effectExplainability: Understand how the model got thereA confident answer with no visible reasoning leaves me nothing to review. Tammy Snow makes the builder’s version of this case in AI Doesn’t Have a Technology Problem. It Has a Human One. She calls for transparent reasoning and reversible actions, because “the system doesn’t know what it doesn’t know,” and treats each override as feedback.Dan Maccarone adds the reviewer’s side in We’re gorging on borrowed trust and it’s going to cost us. One of his clients runs on the rule “people conclude, machines don’t,” and he warns that a reviewer who never overrules the machine is a rubber stamp.Rubber stamps are dangerous, AI or not.Make Financial DecisionsA large language model isn’t a large mathematical model: it predicts likely text, so even one that gets a sum right 95% of the time is wrong once in every 20 tries. For a draft, 95% is a good day, but for a calculation it isn’t good enough.When I use a model for money at all, it writes the spreadsheet formulas, and the spreadsheet does the math.Choosing what to do with the numbers stays with me.The outcome shows up years later and turns on things a model can’t see, like how much risk I can live with.AI is pretty low on the list. I’m aligned with that.In Gallup’s Where Americans and Canadians Turn for Financial Guidance (2026), 18% of U.S. adults seeking financial guidance in the past year had used artificial intelligence tools.By contrast, 32% had at least some confidence in financial advisers.Access My Sensitive DataCustomer contracts, personnel records, passwords, and anything a client trusted my team to protect never go into a model I don’t control. In legal tech, the contract data belonged to the customer, and that habit stuck.Deciding who sees a record is a judgment call, and sending it has no undo. Depending on a tool’s terms, what I paste can end up in training data and surface later in someone else’s answer. In Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models (2020), researchers got GPT-2 to repeat memorized training text word for word, including names, phone numbers, and email addresses.Once a record leaves the building, no review after the fact brings it back.In IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report (2025), one in five organizations reported a breach due to shadow AI, meaning tools employees used without approval. Heavy shadow AI use added $670,000 to average breach costs.Sensitive work stays in tools my company has approved and the vendors have locked down.Get Psychological AdviceWhen I need advice about stress, a conflict at work, or my own state of mind, I go to people.A model can explain burnout, since the literature offers a guideline. What to do about my own life depends on things I may not say out loud.Models also lean toward agreeing with whoever is typing. In Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence (2025), researchers tested 11 leading models and found they affirmed users’ actions 50% more than humans did.In a live experiment, people who got the flattering answers grew more convinced they were right and less willing to repair a conflict. They also rated the flattering answers higher.Good advice sometimes tells you you’re wrong, and a model tuned to please rarely will.A friend, a mentor, or a licensed therapist knows me over time and can push back when I’m the one causing the trouble.A drafted message waiting on a laptop screen, a hand resting just short of the send button.Send Final Messages in My NameA model can draft an email or a Slack reply, and I’ll edit it like any other draft. What it doesn’t get is the send button. A message to my team, my manager, or a customer carries my name and my relationships, and once it goes out, there’s no undo.People can tell, and it costs something.In Study uncovers social cost of using AI in conversations, Cornell University researchers paired 219 pairs of people in chats where smart replies were available.When people believed their partner was leaning on the suggested replies, they rated that partner as less cooperative and felt less connected to them.A message in my name is something I own, and a model can’t make promises for me.Agents raise the stakes, since they can send on their own schedule, many times before anyone reads the log. So a model drafts, and I read, edit, and press send. The person on the other end is deciding whether to trust me.Set Your Own GuidelinesThe first group grows every few months as skills, scripts, and search tools improve. I’ll keep moving work across the line, and I’ll check each move by clicking, running, or reading.The second group hasn’t moved, and I don’t expect it to.Making financial decisions, guarding sensitive data, getting psychological advice, and sending final messages in my name have no guideline or can’t be undone.So here’s the test I’d give any designer, product manager, or researcher sorting through their own week. Run each task through these three questions first:Name the guideline. If nothing outside the work can check it, the task is a decision, so keep it, however good the model’s draft looks.Check who wrote it. If you wrote the guideline yourself, hand the work over, then review everything that comes back against it.Find the signature. If your name is on the result, or it must be right 100% of the time, keep the whole task yourself.Your groups will probably look a little different from mine. That’s fine, as long as you can name the guideline for every job in the first one.I let AI build. I don’t let AI decide. was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
